title: At everyday speeds, the loss is tiny
spoken: At small speed, the clock's fractional loss per coordinate second approaches one half v squared over c squared.
explanation: The moving clock falls behind by 1 − 1/γ of each stationary-system second. For speeds much smaller than c that fraction is about half of v²/c²: at 300 m/s, about five parts in ten million million.
assumptions: A clock and a rod at rest in the moving system, which moves at speed v relative to the stationary system, with |v| < c.
Speeds much smaller than the speed of light; the approximation drops terms in the fourth power of v/c.

notes.title: Half of it
notes.explanation: The first term of the expansion of 1 − 1/γ for small v/c.

notes.title: c squared
notes.explanation: The square of the speed of light.

notes.title: What it falls behind
notes.explanation: One minus its rate: the part of each second the moving clock does not record.

notes.title: The clock's rate
notes.explanation: One over gamma: the fraction of a stationary-system second that passes on the moving clock.

notes.title: v squared over c squared
notes.explanation: For everyday speeds this is a very small number.

notes.title: Approximately equal
notes.explanation: Exact only in the limit of small speed. At 0.6c the left side is 0.2 and the right side 0.18.

notes.title: v squared
notes.explanation: The loss does not depend on the direction of motion.

notes.title: Lorentz factor
notes.explanation: One over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared: 1 at rest, larger at any speed, without limit as v approaches c. The paper writes it as beta.

notes.title: Speed of light
notes.explanation: The paper's V. It enters because both systems must find the same speed for light.

notes.title: Speed of the moving system
notes.explanation: The speed of k relative to K. Its sign gives the direction.
